summary: Discusses techniques applications have used to check and transform domain names, especially to deduce top-level domains from partial information. New top-level domains exposed flaws in some of these methods that make parts of the Internet harder or impossible to reach. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Some programs guess whether something is a valid website name from its ending. When new endings appeared, those guesses broke. This explains how to check names without guessing wrong.

subtitle: How to validate domain names, email addresses, and URLs correctly

tldr.problem: Many applications hardcoded assumptions about domain names like TLDs being only 2-4 characters long. When ICANN introduced new TLDs with different lengths, these applications started rejecting valid domain names.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC draws together the actual DNS and email standards, showing what the protocols actually require. It explains how to check names correctly using the LDH rule for character restrictions, requiring at least one period, and letting DNS itself determine validity rather than maintaining local lists.
tldr.outcome: Developers can write validation that works across past, present and future TLDs by following the standards rather than heuristics. The RFC recommends testing names against actual DNS servers rather than against local TLD lists.

today: RFC 3696 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It remains relevant guidance for applications that validate Internet identifiers, especially as ICANN continues to add new TLDs.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Applications often validate user input before sending it to the network. This helps catch errors early and improves user experience. However, many applications check domain names, email addresses and URLs using rules that are based on old assumptions or are just plain wrong. When the standards evolved, especially when ICANN added new top-level domains like .AERO and .MUSEUM, these applications started rejecting valid addresses, making parts of the Internet unreachable for their users.

This RFC gathers the actual rules from the DNS and email standards in one place, so developers can write correct checks instead of guessing.
sections.eli5: Programs check if addresses look right before trying them. But old checks break with new addresses. This tells you the real rules so your check still works tomorrow.

sections.title: Domain Names: The LDH Rule and Length Limits
sections.content:
DNS names are made of labels separated by periods. Each label can use only ASCII letters, digits, and hyphens (this is called the LDH rule). Hyphens cannot appear at the start or end of a label.

A fully-qualified domain name must contain at least one period, and the complete name cannot exceed 255 octets. Individual labels cannot exceed 63 octets. Top-level domains cannot be all digits.

Before ICANN expanded the TLD list, developers assumed TLDs were always 2, 3, or 4 characters long. This heuristic failed when .MUSEUM and other new TLDs arrived. The RFC warns against building static lists. Instead, use DNS queries to verify that a domain name is actually registered.
sections.eli5: Domain names use letters, numbers, and hyphens. They need a dot in them. Old guesses about how long a domain ending would be broke, so ask the DNS instead of guessing.

sections.title: Email Address Syntax
sections.content:
A valid email address has a local part (before the @) and a domain part (after the @). The domain part follows the same DNS rules as above. The local part is more permissive: it can use many special characters like +, !, $, %, and underscores, either directly or quoted with backslashes.

Examples like user+mailbox@example.com and customer/department=shipping@example.com are all valid. Most applications reject these because they look unusual, but the standards allow them for legitimate purposes like email routing and forwarding.

Length limits are strict: the local part cannot exceed 64 octets, and the domain part cannot exceed 255 octets, for a total maximum of 320 characters.
sections.eli5: Email lets you put unusual special characters in the left side if you know what you are doing. Many programs wrongly reject them. Always let the mail system check, not your program.

sections.title: URLs and Web Address Guessing
sections.content:
HTTP URLs follow a pattern: http://host:port/path?search followed by a fragment (the hash character plus an identifier). Some characters in URLs have special meaning and must be percent-encoded if used as literal characters. The MAILTO URL scheme lets you encode email addresses in a link, but characters valid in email must be percent-encoded to avoid confusion with URL syntax.

Web browsers have adopted heuristics to guess complete URLs from incomplete input. These guesses rely on knowing all valid TLDs. If the browser's TLD list is out of date, it may transform a valid domain name like example.aero into example.aero.com and then fail or find the wrong host.

The RFC warns against such guessing and recommends letting users type complete addresses, or at least making guessing optional and fallible.
sections.eli5: Web browsers try to guess what you meant by what you type. If they do not know all the valid endings, they get it wrong. Better to ask the user or be honest about guessing.

sections.title: Internationalized Domain Names
sections.content:
The IETF introduced IDNA (Internationalized Domain Names in Applications), which lets domain names use non-ASCII characters. The actual DNS stores these names in an encoded form starting with xn--. Applications should accept both the encoded form and the local-script form.

The validation process for IDNA is complex and has no shortcuts: syntax validity is defined only by executing the validation algorithm, not by simple character rules. Each TLD may enforce different rules about which non-ASCII characters are allowed, so client-side validation of international names is unreliable. It is better to let the protocol and remote server make these decisions.
sections.eli5: Domain names can now use letters from other languages. They get encoded with a special prefix in the DNS. Let the server check these, not your program, because the rules are complicated and keep changing.

sections.title: Validation Best Practices
sections.content:
The RFC concludes with a principle: if validation is necessary, do it correctly. Use the LDH rule for character checking, require at least one period in domain names, but then rely on the DNS and the remote protocols to determine actual validity rather than maintaining local lists that become obsolete.

The tradeoff is between early error detection and accepting that users might type something invalid which the protocol itself will reject. If you do validate, follow the standards exactly, and update any local information regularly.
sections.eli5: Check what you can, but trust the real system to say yes or no. Do not try to be smarter than the actual standards.
